blocks.text: The challenge of mapping as-is versus to-be processes

When you start mapping as-is versus to-be processes, you often face a conflict between simplicity and accuracy. If your model is too simple, it misses key edge cases. If it is too complex, it becomes impossible for stakeholders to understand. You must find the middle ground where the model is useful for both developers and business owners.

Many analysts treat modeling as a form of programming. They focus on the syntax of BPMN 2.0 rather than the reality of the process. This often leads to models that do not account for how events change over time. When you lack an execution environment, your static diagrams quickly become shelfware. They stop reflecting the actual work being done in your organization.

items: Ambiguity in requirements gathering leads to incorrect as-is maps.
Lack of domain knowledge prevents accurate representation of current bottlenecks.
Over-engineering the to-be state creates unrealistic expectations for technical teams.
Maintenance is often ignored, causing models to become outdated within months.

blocks.text: You do not need expensive enterprise software to improve your process modeling. Start by decomposing large processes into smaller, manageable chunks. This makes it easier to verify each step with the relevant department head. Use clear, simple notation that anyone in the room can follow, even if they are not familiar with formal modeling standards.
Create a governance plan early. Assign one person to own the model. They must review it every time a major change occurs in the underlying system.

blocks.text: How to stay productive while modeling

The administrative load of documenting these processes is high. You spend hours writing descriptions, updating Jira tickets, and emailing stakeholders. Lazur can help you manage these tasks by voice, keeping your hands on your diagramming tool while you dictate notes or search for requirements.

faq.question: Why do my process models become obsolete?
faq.answer: Models usually become obsolete because they are not integrated into a maintenance cycle. If you do not assign an owner to review the model when the process changes, it will quickly drift from reality.

faq.question: What is the best way to start a to-be process map?
faq.answer: Start by identifying the pain points in your current as-is map. The to-be process should directly address these specific inefficiencies rather than attempting to redesign the entire system from scratch.
